hints: Focus on what type of chloride $\text{SiCl}_4$ is, and remember how Period 3 chlorides behave differently with water.
Write the hydrolysis equation for $\text{SiCl}_4$: it forms solid silicon dioxide, $\text{SiO}_2$, and hydrogen chloride, $\text{HCl}$.
Now link each product to what you would see, a white solid in water and an acidic gas in moist air, to pick the observation that has both.
walkthrough:
**Recall hydrolysis of covalent chlorides**

Think of $\text{SiCl}_4$ as a covalent, tetrahedral chloride that is readily attacked by water. Unlike $\text{CCl}_4$, silicon can expand its octet so hydrolysis is vigorous and complete.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{SiCl}_4(l) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{SiO}_2(s) + 4\text{HCl}(g)$$

**Identify the white precipitate**

One product is silicon dioxide, $\text{SiO}_2$. This is an insoluble white solid, so it appears as a white precipitate in the beaker.

**Identify the steamy fumes**

The other product is hydrogen chloride, $\text{HCl}$. This gas dissolves in moist air to form tiny droplets of hydrochloric acid, which we see as dense white steamy fumes. Since we get both a solid and a fumes-forming gas, both observations occur together.

options.A: Not correct. No reaction is the behaviour of $\text{CCl}_4$, which cannot expand its octet. $\text{SiCl}_4$ hydrolyses vigorously, so you do see changes.
options.B: Correct. $\text{SiCl}_4$ hydrolyses to give $\text{SiO}_2(s)$, seen as a white precipitate, and $\text{HCl}(g)$, seen as steamy white fumes in moist air.
options.C: Incomplete. A white precipitate of $\text{SiO}_2$ does form, but this misses the second product. The $\text{HCl}$ gas also gives very obvious steamy fumes.
options.D: Incomplete. Steamy fumes of $\text{HCl}$ are indeed seen, but this misses the second product. The insoluble $\text{SiO}_2$ also forms a white precipitate.
